cards-func#2.en: h is the hyperbola  h(x) = 6/(x + 2) + 1.  B is the point where h cuts the x-axis.

cards-func#3.en: f is the hyperbola  f(x) = 4/(x + 1) + 2.  Its asymptotes are x = −1 and y = 2.

cards-func#4.en: h is the hyperbola  h(x) = 6/(x + 2) + 1.  Its asymptotes are x = −2 and y = 1, and h cuts the x-axis at B(−8 ; 0).

cards-func#6.en: f is the parabola  f(x) = −x² + 6x + 7  and g is the line  g(x) = 2x + 2.  The two graphs cut each other at A(−1 ; 0) and at C, and A is also the x-intercept of both graphs. PQ is a line segment drawn parallel to the y-axis, with P on f and Q on g, and with PQ lying between A and C.

func-graphs-together#1.en:
f(x) = −x² + 6x + 7  and  g(x) = 2x + 2. The two graphs cut each other at A(−1 ; 0) and at C. A is also the x-intercept of both graphs.
PQ is a line segment drawn parallel to the y-axis, with P on f and Q on g, and with PQ lying between A and C.

Determine the range of f.

func-graphs-together#2.en: Look at the sign of a first — that tells you whether this parabola is happy or sad, and therefore whether the range runs upwards or downwards. Then you need the one y-value it turns at.

func-graphs-together#3.en: a = −1 < 0, so f is a sad parabola: it has a maximum, and the range runs from that maximum downwards. So find the turning point.

func-graphs-together#6.en: WATCH OUT: the range is a statement about y, so it must be written in y. Writing x ≤ 16 here scores nothing.

func-graphs-together#7.en: Range means “which y-values does this graph actually reach”. A parabola only ever turns once, so its turning point is the ceiling or the floor of everything it does — and which of the two depends entirely on the sign of a. Here a is negative, so the arms point down: the graph climbs to the turning point and then falls away forever, which makes that y-value the highest it ever gets and everything below it reachable. So the range is “y less than or equal to the turning y-value”. Notice you only need the y of the turning point for a range question — the x is just the road you travel to get there.

func-graphs-together#8.en: Determine the maximum length of PQ.

func-graphs-together#9.en: PQ is vertical, so its length is one graph's y-value minus the other's — top minus bottom. Write that difference down as a single new expression and look at what kind of graph it is.

func-graphs-together#10.en: PQ is vertical, so its length is simply top graph minus bottom graph. Between A and C the parabola is on top.

func-graphs-together#13.en: That is a brand-new sad parabola, so the longest PQ sits at its turning point:

func-graphs-together#16.en: WATCH OUT: length is never negative. If you subtract the wrong way round you get x² − 4x − 5 and a minimum of −9 — the minus sign is the warning that the graphs were the wrong way round.

func-graphs-together#17.en: The fact you have to fetch here is that the gap between two graphs is itself a graph. PQ is not a fixed length; it depends on where you draw it, so write it as a formula in x — f(x) minus g(x) — and suddenly you are holding a brand-new parabola whose height at every x IS the length of PQ there. Finding the longest PQ is then just finding that new parabola's maximum, which is the same x = −b/(2a) move you have used all year. Two cautions. First, top minus bottom, in that order, or your “length” comes out negative. Second, do not go hunting for a Grade 12 tool — the difference parabola plus −b/(2a) is all this needs. Bank the earlier marks first: finish (a) and everything in Questions 1 to 4 before you sit down with this one.

func-graphs-together#18.en: Determine the value(s) of t for which the equation f(x) = t will have two unequal positive roots.

func-graphs-together#19.en: f(x) = t is a horizontal line y = t sliding up and down across f, and the roots are where it cuts. Ask the question twice: how high may the line go before it stops cutting twice, and how low may it drop before one of the cuts crosses to the left of the y-axis?

func-graphs-together#20.en: f(x) = t is the horizontal line y = t sliding up and down across f. The roots are where that line cuts the parabola, so the question is really: where must the line sit? Two conditions, one at a time.

func-graphs-together#21.en: Two unequal roots. The line must cut f twice, so it has to stay below the maximum:  t < 16

func-graphs-together#22.en: Both roots positive. Both cutting points must lie to the right of the y-axis. f cuts the y-axis at f(0) = 7, so the line has to sit above that:  t > 7

func-graphs-together#23.en: At t = 7 exactly, one root is x = 0 — and zero is not positive. Below 7, one root turns negative.

func-graphs-together#25.en: REMEMBER: the two facts you needed — the maximum 16 and the y-intercept 7 — are nowhere in the question. On a starred part, that is always the job: work out what the sketch knows before you try to answer.

func-graphs-together#26.en: Do not solve −x² + 6x + 7 = t for x here; picture it instead. The equation f(x) = t is asking where a flat line at height t meets the curve, so slide that line in your head. Up at the very top, at the turning point, the line touches once — that is equal roots, not two unequal ones — and above that it misses entirely, so t has to stay under 16. Now slide it down. As the line drops, the left-hand cut travels left, and the moment the line passes through the y-intercept at 7 that left cut lands exactly on x = 0. Zero is not positive, so 7 is out and anything lower is worse. Squeeze the two conditions together and the line has to live strictly between them. Both numbers, 16 and 7, had to be worked out from the equation of f — the question never handed you either one, which is precisely why this part carries the star.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#1.en:
The graph of f is defined by  f(x) = 4/(x + 1) + 2.

Write down the equations of the asymptotes of f.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#2.en: Line the equation up against the standard shape y = a/(x − p) + q and read p and q straight off. Look hard at the sign in the denominator.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#3.en: Read the form off first:  f(x) = a/(x − p) + q  with  a = 4,  p = −1,  q = 2. The vertical asymptote is x = p and the horizontal asymptote is y = q.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#5.en: WATCH OUT: (x + 1) in the denominator means p = −1, not +1 — the bracket always shows the opposite sign. Same trap as the turning point of a parabola.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#6.en: The asymptotes are the two lines the graph creeps towards but never touches, and both are already sitting in the equation once you line it up with the standard shape. The vertical one comes from the denominator: x + 1 is zero at x = −1, and dividing by zero is the one thing the graph cannot do, so it goes around that line forever. The horizontal one is the + 2 on the end. Make the fraction as tiny as you like by pushing x out towards infinity, and what is left is 2 — so the graph settles towards y = 2 without ever arriving. The sign flip on p is the only place marks go missing: the standard form says (x − p), so a bracket reading (x + 1) means p is negative one.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#7.en: Determine the equation of the axis of symmetry of f that has a negative gradient.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#8.en: Both axes of symmetry go through the point where the asymptotes cross — x = −1 and y = 2, so that point is (−1 ; 2). A negative gradient on a hyperbola means one particular value; put it and the point into y = mx + c.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#9.en: Both axes of symmetry go through the point where the asymptotes cross, (−1 ; 2). The one with a negative gradient is y = −x + c:

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#12.en: WATCH OUT: the centre is (−1 ; 2), not (1 ; 2). Substitute the point you actually read off the asymptotes, and substitute it with its own signs.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#13.en: REMEMBER: every hyperbola has two axes of symmetry through (p ; q) — y = x + c and y = −x + c. Read which one the question wants before you start.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#14.en: A hyperbola's two mirror lines are the diagonals through the corner where the asymptotes meet — one rising at 45°, one falling at 45°. That is why their gradients are always exactly 1 and −1, whatever a happens to be, and why “the one with a negative gradient” picks one out without any further information. From there it is Grade 9 work: you have a gradient and a point on the line, so put them into y = mx + c and solve for c. The one place to slow down is substituting a negative x into −x, which turns into +1 — write the brackets in rather than doing it in your head.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#15.en:
The graph of h is obtained by shifting the graph of f two units to the LEFT and four units DOWN.
Write down the equation of h.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#16.en: Handle the two shifts separately, and in the right places: a sideways shift happens inside the bracket, a vertical one outside. The sideways direction is the one that feels backwards.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#17.en: Two units to the left replaces x by x + 2:

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#19.en: Four units down subtracts 4 from the whole thing:

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#21.en: WATCH OUT: LEFT is +2 inside the bracket. It feels backwards and it is not: the whole picture slides left, so every x has to be fed a bigger number to land where it used to. Down is −4 outside, where it behaves the way you expect.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#22.en: The reason a horizontal shift looks inside-out is worth getting straight once, because it comes back every year. The graph does not move because x changes; the graph moves because you have changed what the machine does to each x. Slide the picture two units left and the point that used to sit above x = 0 now sits above x = −2 — so to get the old output at the new place, the machine has to add 2 to whatever it is handed first. Hence x + 2 inside. A vertical shift has no such trickery: after the machine has finished, you simply take 4 off the answer, so the −4 sits outside and does exactly what it says. A quick sanity check on your answer: the asymptotes should have moved the same way as the graph, and they have — x = −1 became x = −3, and y = 2 became y = −2.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#23.en: Determine the values of x for which  h(x) < −2.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#24.en: Look at what −2 actually is for h — you worked it out in (c). Get one side to zero rather than multiplying anything across, then cut the line at the asymptote and paint each section.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#25.en: −2 is exactly h's horizontal asymptote, so the question is really “where does h lie below its own asymptote?”

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#27.en: 4 is positive, so the fraction can only be negative when the denominator is negative. Cut the line at the asymptote x = −3 and paint each side: left of −3 the fraction is − (h is below y = −2), right of −3 it is + (h is above y = −2).

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#28.en: the painted − section is the left one:  x + 3 < 0  ⟹  x < −3

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#29.en: WATCH OUT: never multiply an inequality by (x + 3) — you do not know whether it is positive or negative, so you do not know whether to turn the sign around. Get one side to 0, then paint the sections.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#30.en: Two small ideas do all the work. The first is noticing that −2 is not a random number: it is h's own horizontal asymptote, so subtracting it wipes out the whole tail of the expression and leaves a bare fraction. That is why the inequality collapses to “when is 4/(x + 3) negative?” instead of turning into anything messy. The second is her paint method. A fraction can only change sign where its top is zero or its bottom is zero, so you cut the line at those places — here only at the asymptote x = −3 — and then each section can be painted with a single + or − because nothing inside a section can change. The top is a fixed positive 4, so the sign of the whole fraction is simply the sign of the bottom: negative to the left of −3, positive to the right. Read the painted − section off and you are done. And notice the answer has no closed end — x = −3 is an asymptote, so it can never be included.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#31.en: Determine the values of k for which the line  y = −x + k  will NOT cut the graph of f.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#32.en: “Does not cut” is a statement about how many solutions the two equations have together. Set them equal, clear the fraction to get an ordinary quadratic, and then think about what the discriminant has to do.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#33.en: “Does not cut” means the two equations have no real solution together. So set them equal and force the discriminant negative.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#35.en: 2x + 6 = −x² − x + kx + k  ⟹  x² + (3 − k)x + (6 − k) = 0

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#36.en: No real roots means Δ < 0:  Δ = (3 − k)² − 4(1)(6 − k) = 9 − 6k + k² − 24 + 4k = k² − 2k − 15 = (k − 5)(k + 3)

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#38.en: WATCH OUT: Δ < 0, not Δ ≤ 0. At k = −3 and at k = 5 the discriminant is zero, which means equal roots — the line touches the graph once. Touching is still meeting, so those two values must be left out.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#39.en: REMEMBER: “does not cut” = “no real solution” = Δ < 0. It is the same sentence you use on a parabola-and-line question; the only extra step here is clearing the fraction first.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential-2#40.en: The fact you have to fetch is that “cutting” and “solving” are the same thing said two ways. Wherever the line meets the curve, both equations are true at once, so setting them equal turns a picture question into an algebra question — and once the fraction is cleared it is an ordinary quadratic. Now the discriminant is doing what it always does: two real roots means two crossings, one repeated root means the line just touches, and no real roots means the line and the curve never meet at all. The question asked for the last case, so Δ has to be strictly negative. Two details decide the marks. The first is the strictness — at Δ = 0 the line grazes the graph, and grazing counts as meeting, so the endpoints are out. The second is what happens after you factorise Δ: (k − 5)(k + 3) < 0 is itself a quadratic inequality, so it is a happy parabola in k and “less than zero” is the inside of the bowl, between −3 and 5. Bank the earlier marks first — (a) to (d) are all straightforward, and this is the one to come back to.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#1.en:
h is a hyperbola. Its asymptotes are the lines x = −2 and y = 1. The graph passes through the point A(0 ; 4) and cuts the x-axis at B.

Determine the equation of h.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#2.en: Start from the shape y = a/(x − p) + q and read p and q straight off the asymptotes — watch the sign on p. That leaves only one unknown, and you have been handed a point to pin it down with.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#3.en: A hyperbola is y = a/(x − p) + q, with the asymptotes at x = p and y = q. Read them straight off:

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#6.en: The one thing still unknown is a, so use the point that was given, A(0 ; 4):

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#9.en: WATCH OUT: p is the opposite sign of the number sitting next to the x. The asymptote x = −2 gives (x + 2) in the denominator, not (x − 2).

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#10.en: Every hyperbola in Grade 11 is the same basic curve, y = a/x, picked up and moved: p slides it sideways, q slides it up or down, and a decides how far the branches sit from the corner. The asymptotes are the crosshairs of that move, so they hand you p and q for free — as long as you remember the sign flip on p, because the equation says (x − p) and the asymptote says x = p. With p and q in, only a is left, and one point on the curve is exactly enough to find one unknown: put the point's x and y in and solve. That is the whole three-step pattern for finding a hyperbola's equation, and it is the same pattern as finding a parabola's — read off what the picture gives you, then use a point for whatever is left over.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#11.en: Write down the domain of h.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#12.en: Domain is the x-values that are allowed. There is exactly one x this graph cannot cope with — find it by asking what would make the denominator zero.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#13.en: The graph is undefined where the denominator is zero: x + 2 = 0.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#15.en: Domain means “which x-values may I feed in”. For a hyperbola the answer is always “all of them except the one that breaks the fraction”, and that one is the vertical asymptote — the same x = −2 that's h's own asymptote. Note how it is written: all the real numbers first, then the restriction riding after a semicolon. That semicolon-then-restriction layout is the one she marks.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#17.en: B is on the x-axis. What is y worth at every single point of the x-axis? Put that into the equation for h and solve.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#18.en: B is on the x-axis, so y = 0:

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#21.en: WATCH OUT: the answer must be a coordinate, written with a semicolon: (−8 ; 0). The comma belongs to decimals only.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#22.en: An x-intercept is not a special formula to memorise — it is just the point where the graph is sitting on the x-axis, and every point on the x-axis has y = 0. So you substitute 0 for y and solve the equation you are left with. The only fiddly bit is that the x you want is stuck in a denominator; getting the fraction alone on one side first, before you cross-multiply, keeps that tidy. And because the question asked for the COORDINATES of B, the answer has to be a point, not just a number.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#23.en: Determine the equation of the axis of symmetry of h that has a positive gradient.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#24.en: Both axes of symmetry go through the point where the two asymptotes cross. You know that point, and you have been told the gradient is positive — for a hyperbola that means exactly one value.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#25.en: Both axes of symmetry pass through the point where the asymptotes cross, which is (−2 ; 1). The one with a positive gradient has m = 1:

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#28.en: REMEMBER: the other one is y = −x + c through the same point, giving y = −x − 1. Both go through (p ; q) — only the gradient tells them apart.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#29.en: A hyperbola has two mirror lines, and they are the two diagonals through the corner where the asymptotes meet — one going up at 45°, one going down at 45°. That is why their gradients are always exactly 1 and −1, no matter what a is, and why “the one with a positive gradient” is enough information to pick one out. From there it is a plain Grade 9 job: you have a gradient and a point, so put them into y = mx + c and solve for c.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#30.en: For which values of x is h(x) ≤ 0?

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#31.en: Cut a line through every x-intercept and every asymptote, then paint the sign of h on each piece. Think carefully about which of your two cut points may be included in the answer and which may never be.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#32.en: Cut a line through every x-intercept and every asymptote — here x = −8 and x = −2 — then paint the sign of h on each piece:

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#33.en: left of −8:  +   ·   between −8 and −2:  −   ·   right of −2:  +

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#34.en: h(x) ≤ 0 is the painted − piece.  x = −8 is included, because h(−8) = 0.  x = −2 is never included — h is undefined there.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#36.en: WATCH OUT: never close the bracket on an asymptote. −8 ≤ x ≤ −2 loses the mark, because h(−2) does not exist.

func-hyperbola-and-exponential#37.en: A graph can only change from positive to negative in two ways: by crossing the x-axis, or by jumping across an asymptote. So the cut lines go through exactly those places, and between two cuts the sign cannot change at all — which means one glance at each piece settles the whole piece. Paint a + or a − on each and the answer reads straight off. The last decision is about the ends. At an x-intercept the graph really is zero, and “≤ 0” includes zero, so that end is closed. At an asymptote the graph does not exist at all, so that end can never be closed, no matter which inequality sign the question used. One end closed, one end open, in the same answer — that is the shape this question is built to test.

leftovers.text: f is the parabola  f(x) = 2x² − 6x − 8,  with turning point TP(1,5 ; −12,5).
h is the hyperbola  h(x) = 6/(x + 2) + 1.  Its asymptotes are x = −2 and y = 1.
